The recurrence \(|A_i| = |A_{i-1}| + |A_{i-2}|\) holds only after accounting for the special role of the number 1, which creates a self‑loop ( \(1\to2\to1\) ).  
Because 1 appears with \(S(1)=2\), its even predecessor 2 (which has \(S(2)=1\)) must be excluded from the construction of \(A_3\), and its odd predecessor 1 must be excluded from the construction of \(A_4\).  

Correcting for these two exclusions gives the exact counts:

\[
\begin{aligned}
|A_1| &= 1 \quad (n=2)\\
|A_2| &= 2 \quad (n=1,4)\\
|A_3| &= |A_2|+|A_1|-1 = 2\\
|A_4| &= |A_3|+|A_2|-1 = 3\\
|A_5| &= |A_4|+|A_3| = 5\\
|A_6| &= |A_5|+|A_4| = 8\\
|A_7| &= 13,\; |A_8| = 21,\; |A_9| = 34,\; |A_{10}| = 55,\; |A_{11}| = 89.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the number of positive integers \(n\) with \(S(n)=11\) is **89**, not 144.

**VERDICT: REJECT**
